title: Algebra: Quantities, Equations, and Structure
subtitle: From Arithmetic Readiness Through Radicals and Logarithms
centralStory: Algebra is the art of preserving meaning while changing representation.

units.title: Arithmetic Readiness and Repair
units.act: Prologue - Making quantity dependable
units.role: Adaptive support layer with complete instruction for students who need numerical repair.
units.governingQuestion: What must be dependable about numbers before symbols can carry meaning?
units.storyArc: The learner stabilizes numerical meaning: signed quantities, multiplicative structure, fractions, rates, units, powers, and roots. Diagnostic routing allows a student to enter only the pages needed and then return to the main Algebra spine.
outcomes: Interpret signed numbers as position, direction, and change.
Compute with whole numbers, fractions, decimals, and percentages while estimating plausibility.
Use factors, multiples, ratios, rates, and units structurally.
Interpret powers and roots and use scientific notation.
Recognize when arithmetic output is unreasonable or dimensionally impossible.
units.investigation: Compare several phone, grocery, or subscription plans using estimation, rates, percentages, units, and exact calculations.
units.mastery: A ten-domain diagnostic routes each missed strand to one repair lesson followed by a short return check.

units.title: Quantities, Variables, and Mathematical Objects
units.act: Act I - Giving general names to quantities
units.role: Establish what algebra describes before asking students to manipulate it.
units.governingQuestion: How can symbols name quantities and relationships without erasing their meaning?
units.storyArc: Concrete quantities become tables, graphs, verbal rules, expressions, equations, and inequalities. Students learn what kind of object each notation represents and how substitution preserves structure.
outcomes: Identify changing, fixed, unknown, and parameter quantities.
Translate among verbal, numerical, graphical, and symbolic representations.
Distinguish expressions, equations, and inequalities.
Parse terms, factors, coefficients, and grouping structure.
Substitute and evaluate while preserving units and parentheses.
units.investigation: Model equipment rental cost using a context, table, graph preview, expression, and equation.
units.mastery: Students classify mathematical objects, translate representations, and evaluate formulas with signed inputs and units.

units.title: Expressions, Equality, and Linear Equations
units.act: Act II - Preserving truth while changing form
units.role: Build the central equivalence engine of elementary algebra.
units.governingQuestion: How can an equation change form without changing its solutions?
units.storyArc: Students first test solutions, then use inverse operations and simplification to construct equivalent equations. The unit ends with strategy selection and one-variable modeling.
outcomes: Define a solution and solution set.
Construct equivalent linear equations using legal operations.
Solve equations containing parentheses, fractions, decimals, and variables on both sides.
Recognize identities and contradictions.
Build and check one-variable models.
units.investigation: Reconstruct an original quantity after a sequence of fees, discounts, or changes.
units.mastery: Mixed equations without method labels; students must show an equivalence-preserving chain and verify the result.

units.title: Inequalities, Absolute Value, and Formulas
units.act: Act III - Describing regions and constraints
units.role: Extend algebra from exact equality to ranges, distance conditions, and reusable formulas.
units.governingQuestion: How do we describe all values satisfying a condition?
units.storyArc: Equation methods are adapted to inequalities; negative scaling reveals order reversal; intervals describe regions; absolute value becomes distance; formulas are rearranged without assigning numerical values.
outcomes: Interpret and graph inequality solution sets.
Explain why multiplication or division by a negative reverses order.
Translate among inequality, interval, and number-line forms.
Solve compound and absolute-value inequalities.
Rearrange formulas and preserve units.
units.investigation: Represent manufacturing tolerance or acceptable measurement error in words, inequalities, intervals, graphs, and absolute value.
units.mastery: Students solve, graph, and interpret mixed inequalities and rearrange formulas with units.

units.title: Ratios, Rates, and Linear Relationships
units.act: Act IV - Turning constant change into lines
units.role: Connect proportional reasoning, slope, equations, graphs, and linear models.
units.governingQuestion: How do two quantities change together at a constant rate?
units.storyArc: Ratios become unit rates, proportionality becomes a line through the origin, and slope generalizes constant rate. Multiple line forms reveal different information; data modeling distinguishes exact relationships from approximate trends.
outcomes: Use ratios, unit rates, proportions, and percent multipliers.
Interpret a graph as a set of ordered-pair solutions.
Calculate and interpret intercepts and slope with units.
Write line equations from points, graphs, and contexts.
Fit, interpret, and critique elementary linear models.
units.investigation: Analyze a real cost, consumption, or public-data set and defend a linear model with a reasonable domain and limitations.
units.mastery: Students move among context, table, graph, and formula and explain slope and intercept with units.

units.title: Systems and Simultaneous Constraints
units.act: Act V - Satisfying several conditions at once
units.role: Extend linear reasoning to multiple equations, variables, and feasible regions.
units.governingQuestion: Which values satisfy several requirements simultaneously?
units.storyArc: Intersections represent simultaneous truth. Graphing estimates solutions, substitution replaces equals by equals, elimination combines equations to remove a variable, and applications reveal when two variables are the natural model.
outcomes: Interpret a system solution as satisfying every constraint.
Solve systems graphically, by substitution, and by elimination.
Classify one, zero, or infinitely many solutions.
Model totals, mixtures, rates, and break-even situations.
Graph systems of inequalities and interpret feasible regions.
units.investigation: Design a production or allocation plan subject to budget, time, and minimum-output constraints.
units.mastery: Mixed systems require method selection and interpretation of the ordered-pair solution.

units.title: Exponents, Roots, and Power Structure
units.act: Act VI - Leaving constant additive change
units.role: Introduce repeated multiplication, its inverse questions, and the first nonlinear families.
units.governingQuestion: How do repeated multiplication and roots create new structures?
units.storyArc: Exponent laws are derived from repeated factors; zero and negative exponents preserve those laws; roots reverse powers; simple power equations and graphs reveal behavior unlike lines.
outcomes: Interpret integer exponents and negative bases.
Derive and apply exponent laws.
Explain zero and negative exponents.
Interpret roots and solve simple power equations.
Compare linear, quadratic, cubic, and root patterns.
units.investigation: Compare additive and power-based scaling in area, volume, and measurement contexts.
units.mastery: Students justify exponent laws from repeated multiplication and solve mixed exact power/root equations.

units.title: Polynomial Operations and Special Products
units.act: Act VII - Building expressions from powers
units.role: Develop the forward multiplication machinery needed for factoring and quadratics.
units.governingQuestion: How can expressions built from powers be combined systematically?
units.storyArc: Polynomials are classified and evaluated, then combined through distribution. Product grids and geometry reveal special products. Division completes the reversible arithmetic of polynomials.
outcomes: Classify and evaluate polynomials.
Add, subtract, and multiply polynomials.
Use exponent laws within monomial operations.
Recognize binomial squares and difference-of-squares products.
Perform polynomial division and verify by multiplication.
units.investigation: Represent the same polynomial product with distribution, a product grid, and an area model.
units.mastery: Mixed polynomial operations with missing powers, signs, and verification by reverse operations.

units.title: Factoring and Quadratic Equations
units.act: Act VIII - Revealing hidden multiplication
units.role: Use reverse multiplication to expose zeros and develop the full quadratic-solving toolkit.
units.governingQuestion: How can hidden product structure reveal solutions?
units.storyArc: Factoring reverses distribution, then the zero-product property turns factors into solutions. Square roots, completing the square, and the quadratic formula provide increasingly general methods, culminating in strategic choice.
outcomes: Factor using GCF, grouping, trinomial, and special-product methods.
Determine whether factoring is complete in the chosen number system.
Solve quadratics by factoring and the square-root method.
Complete the square geometrically and algebraically.
Derive and use the quadratic formula and discriminant.
units.investigation: Choose the most efficient method for a mixed set of quadratic equations and defend each choice.
units.mastery: Students must solve, check, and justify method selection across all four major techniques.

units.title: Quadratic Functions and Models
units.act: Act IX - One nonlinear object, several useful forms
units.role: Connect quadratic equations to parabola geometry, modeling, and optimization.
units.governingQuestion: What does each algebraic form reveal about a parabola?
units.storyArc: The same quadratic appears in standard, factored, and vertex forms. Students learn to choose a form based on the information needed, then use parabolas for modeling, inequalities, and regression.
outcomes: Identify vertex, axis, intercepts, opening, and extremum.
Interpret standard, factored, and vertex forms.
Convert among forms strategically.
Build and interpret quadratic models.
Solve quadratic inequalities and critique quadratic fits.
units.investigation: Build and optimize an area, revenue, or projectile model and interpret all mathematically valid roots.
units.mastery: Students select and convert forms, graph from structure, solve inequalities, and interpret an optimum with units.

units.title: Rational Expressions, Equations, and Variation
units.act: Act X - Tracking where division is allowed
units.role: Develop algebra with variable denominators, explicit restrictions, and inverse variation.
units.governingQuestion: What changes when a variable expression appears in a denominator?
units.storyArc: A denominator creates excluded inputs. Factoring enables cancellation but cannot restore missing domain points. Common denominators permit addition and equation solving; sign analysis introduces rational inequalities and discontinuities.
outcomes: Identify excluded values and preserve original restrictions.
Simplify and perform arithmetic with rational expressions.
Solve rational equations and check candidate solutions.
Simplify complex rational expressions.
Model variation and interpret holes and asymptotes informally.
units.investigation: Compare equivalent-looking rational formulas and explain how a missing input changes the graph or context.
units.mastery: Every answer must include restrictions and rational-equation candidates must be checked in the original equation.

units.title: Radicals, Rational Exponents, and Complex Numbers
units.shortTitle: Radicals, Rational Exponents, and Complex Numbers
units.act: Act XI - Reversing powers and enlarging the number system
units.role: Develop exact root arithmetic, radical equations, extraneous-solution logic, and basic complex arithmetic.
units.governingQuestion: How do we reverse powers, and what happens when the real numbers are insufficient?
units.storyArc: General roots and rational exponents express inverse powers. Radical arithmetic creates exact forms, conjugates rationalize denominators, and raising powers solves equations but may introduce candidates. Complex numbers complete quadratic solutions.
outcomes: Interpret principal and general roots.
Simplify and combine radical expressions.
Rationalize denominators using factors or conjugates.
Connect radicals and rational exponents.
Solve radical equations and perform basic complex arithmetic.
units.investigation: Compare reversible and nonreversible algebraic steps and explain exactly where extraneous candidates enter.
units.mastery: Students preserve domains, simplify exact forms, check radical candidates, and express nonreal quadratic roots correctly.

units.title: Functions as a Unifying Language
units.act: Act XII - Organizing algebra around input and output
units.role: Consolidate earlier relationships into function language without preempting full Precalculus theory.
units.governingQuestion: How can one input-output framework organize the algebraic families already studied?
units.storyArc: Relations become functions when each input has one output. Function notation separates evaluation from solving; domain and range collect restrictions and outputs; piecewise functions and arithmetic unify earlier examples.
outcomes: Determine whether a relation is a function.
Evaluate functions and solve output equations.
Determine domain and range from formulas, graphs, and contexts.
Interpret graph behavior and piecewise rules.
Combine functions arithmetically while tracking domain.
units.investigation: Choose among linear, quadratic, rational, radical, and exponential models for unlabeled data or graphs.
units.mastery: Students move among table, graph, formula, and context and distinguish evaluation from solving.

units.title: Exponential and Logarithmic Algebra
units.act: Act XIII - Describing multiplicative change and undoing it
units.role: Complete the Algebra course with repeated proportional change, inverse exponentiation, and equation solving.
units.governingQuestion: How do we describe multiplicative change and solve for an unknown exponent?
units.storyArc: Constant differences are contrasted with constant ratios. Repeated percentages produce exponential models, compounding motivates e, and logarithms reverse exponentiation. Log laws follow from exponent laws and solve previously inaccessible equations.
outcomes: Distinguish additive from multiplicative patterns.
Construct and interpret exponential growth and decay models.
Use compound and continuous growth formulas.
Define logarithms as inverse exponentiation and use log laws.
Solve exponential and logarithmic equations with domain checks.
units.investigation: Compare linear, exponential, and logarithmic claims made from the same data and decide which conclusions are justified.
units.mastery: Students construct models, solve exact and approximate equations, and reject logarithmic candidates outside the domain.

units.title: Algebra Synthesis and Precalculus Readiness
units.act: Finale - Choosing structure instead of chapter labels
units.role: Turn accumulated techniques into independent classification, strategy, checking, and modeling.
units.governingQuestion: When the problem is unlabeled, how do we decide what structure it has and what method applies?
units.storyArc: Students classify objects and equation families, choose transformations, track implications and restrictions, use technology responsibly, and complete a sustained model that coordinates words, pictures, graphs, and symbols.
outcomes: Classify mathematical objects and equation families.
Choose productive and legal transformations.
Track restrictions, candidates, and extraneous solutions.
Decide between exact, approximate, algebraic, and graphical answers.
Complete a sustained Precalculus-readiness modeling argument.
units.investigation: A final modeling capstone requiring variable definition, diagram, model selection, solution, restrictions, units, graph, sensitivity, and written conclusion.
units.mastery: Readiness requires success across symbolic fluency, representations, explanation, and modeling; a hidden prerequisite failure routes to targeted review.

units.title: Arithmetic Readiness and Repair
units.act: Prologue - Making quantity dependable
units.role: Adaptive support layer with complete instruction for students who need numerical repair.
units.governingQuestion: What must be dependable about numbers before symbols can carry meaning?
units.storyArc: The learner stabilizes numerical meaning: signed quantities, multiplicative structure, fractions, rates, units, powers, and roots. Diagnostic routing allows a student to enter only the pages needed and then return to the main Algebra spine.
outcomes: Interpret signed numbers as position, direction, and change.
Compute with whole numbers, fractions, decimals, and percentages while estimating plausibility.
Use factors, multiples, ratios, rates, and units structurally.
Interpret powers and roots and use scientific notation.
Recognize when arithmetic output is unreasonable or dimensionally impossible.
units.investigation: Compare several phone, grocery, or subscription plans using estimation, rates, percentages, units, and exact calculations.
units.mastery: A ten-domain diagnostic routes each missed strand to one repair lesson followed by a short return check.

units.title: Quantities, Variables, and Mathematical Objects
units.act: Act I - Giving general names to quantities
units.role: Establish what algebra describes before asking students to manipulate it.
units.governingQuestion: How can symbols name quantities and relationships without erasing their meaning?
units.storyArc: Concrete quantities become tables, graphs, verbal rules, expressions, equations, and inequalities. Students learn what kind of object each notation represents and how substitution preserves structure.
outcomes: Identify changing, fixed, unknown, and parameter quantities.
Translate among verbal, numerical, graphical, and symbolic representations.
Distinguish expressions, equations, and inequalities.
Parse terms, factors, coefficients, and grouping structure.
Substitute and evaluate while preserving units and parentheses.
units.investigation: Model equipment rental cost using a context, table, graph preview, expression, and equation.
units.mastery: Students classify mathematical objects, translate representations, and evaluate formulas with signed inputs and units.

units.title: Expressions, Equality, and Linear Equations
units.act: Act II - Preserving truth while changing form
units.role: Build the central equivalence engine of elementary algebra.
units.governingQuestion: How can an equation change form without changing its solutions?
units.storyArc: Students first test solutions, then use inverse operations and simplification to construct equivalent equations. The unit ends with strategy selection and one-variable modeling.
outcomes: Define a solution and solution set.
Construct equivalent linear equations using legal operations.
Solve equations containing parentheses, fractions, decimals, and variables on both sides.
Recognize identities and contradictions.
Build and check one-variable models.
units.investigation: Reconstruct an original quantity after a sequence of fees, discounts, or changes.
units.mastery: Mixed equations without method labels; students must show an equivalence-preserving chain and verify the result.

units.title: Inequalities, Absolute Value, and Formulas
units.act: Act III - Describing regions and constraints
units.role: Extend algebra from exact equality to ranges, distance conditions, and reusable formulas.
units.governingQuestion: How do we describe all values satisfying a condition?
units.storyArc: Equation methods are adapted to inequalities; negative scaling reveals order reversal; intervals describe regions; absolute value becomes distance; formulas are rearranged without assigning numerical values.
outcomes: Interpret and graph inequality solution sets.
Explain why multiplication or division by a negative reverses order.
Translate among inequality, interval, and number-line forms.
Solve compound and absolute-value inequalities.
Rearrange formulas and preserve units.
units.investigation: Represent manufacturing tolerance or acceptable measurement error in words, inequalities, intervals, graphs, and absolute value.
units.mastery: Students solve, graph, and interpret mixed inequalities and rearrange formulas with units.

units.title: Ratios, Rates, and Linear Relationships
units.act: Act IV - Turning constant change into lines
units.role: Connect proportional reasoning, slope, equations, graphs, and linear models.
units.governingQuestion: How do two quantities change together at a constant rate?
units.storyArc: Ratios become unit rates, proportionality becomes a line through the origin, and slope generalizes constant rate. Multiple line forms reveal different information; data modeling distinguishes exact relationships from approximate trends.
outcomes: Use ratios, unit rates, proportions, and percent multipliers.
Interpret a graph as a set of ordered-pair solutions.
Calculate and interpret intercepts and slope with units.
Write line equations from points, graphs, and contexts.
Fit, interpret, and critique elementary linear models.
units.investigation: Analyze a real cost, consumption, or public-data set and defend a linear model with a reasonable domain and limitations.
units.mastery: Students move among context, table, graph, and formula and explain slope and intercept with units.

units.title: Systems and Simultaneous Constraints
units.act: Act V - Satisfying several conditions at once
units.role: Extend linear reasoning to multiple equations, variables, and feasible regions.
units.governingQuestion: Which values satisfy several requirements simultaneously?
units.storyArc: Intersections represent simultaneous truth. Graphing estimates solutions, substitution replaces equals by equals, elimination combines equations to remove a variable, and applications reveal when two variables are the natural model.
outcomes: Interpret a system solution as satisfying every constraint.
Solve systems graphically, by substitution, and by elimination.
Classify one, zero, or infinitely many solutions.
Model totals, mixtures, rates, and break-even situations.
Graph systems of inequalities and interpret feasible regions.
units.investigation: Design a production or allocation plan subject to budget, time, and minimum-output constraints.
units.mastery: Mixed systems require method selection and interpretation of the ordered-pair solution.

units.title: Exponents, Roots, and Power Structure
units.act: Act VI - Leaving constant additive change
units.role: Introduce repeated multiplication, its inverse questions, and the first nonlinear families.
units.governingQuestion: How do repeated multiplication and roots create new structures?
units.storyArc: Exponent laws are derived from repeated factors; zero and negative exponents preserve those laws; roots reverse powers; simple power equations and graphs reveal behavior unlike lines.
outcomes: Interpret integer exponents and negative bases.
Derive and apply exponent laws.
Explain zero and negative exponents.
Interpret roots and solve simple power equations.
Compare linear, quadratic, cubic, and root patterns.
units.investigation: Compare additive and power-based scaling in area, volume, and measurement contexts.
units.mastery: Students justify exponent laws from repeated multiplication and solve mixed exact power/root equations.

units.title: Polynomial Operations and Special Products
units.act: Act VII - Building expressions from powers
units.role: Develop the forward multiplication machinery needed for factoring and quadratics.
units.governingQuestion: How can expressions built from powers be combined systematically?
units.storyArc: Polynomials are classified and evaluated, then combined through distribution. Product grids and geometry reveal special products. Division completes the reversible arithmetic of polynomials.
outcomes: Classify and evaluate polynomials.
Add, subtract, and multiply polynomials.
Use exponent laws within monomial operations.
Recognize binomial squares and difference-of-squares products.
Perform polynomial division and verify by multiplication.
units.investigation: Represent the same polynomial product with distribution, a product grid, and an area model.
units.mastery: Mixed polynomial operations with missing powers, signs, and verification by reverse operations.

units.title: Factoring and Quadratic Equations
units.act: Act VIII - Revealing hidden multiplication
units.role: Use reverse multiplication to expose zeros and develop the full quadratic-solving toolkit.
units.governingQuestion: How can hidden product structure reveal solutions?
units.storyArc: Factoring reverses distribution, then the zero-product property turns factors into solutions. Square roots, completing the square, and the quadratic formula provide increasingly general methods, culminating in strategic choice.
outcomes: Factor using GCF, grouping, trinomial, and special-product methods.
Determine whether factoring is complete in the chosen number system.
Solve quadratics by factoring and the square-root method.
Complete the square geometrically and algebraically.
Derive and use the quadratic formula and discriminant.
units.investigation: Choose the most efficient method for a mixed set of quadratic equations and defend each choice.
units.mastery: Students must solve, check, and justify method selection across all four major techniques.

units.title: Quadratic Functions and Models
units.act: Act IX - One nonlinear object, several useful forms
units.role: Connect quadratic equations to parabola geometry, modeling, and optimization.
units.governingQuestion: What does each algebraic form reveal about a parabola?
units.storyArc: The same quadratic appears in standard, factored, and vertex forms. Students learn to choose a form based on the information needed, then use parabolas for modeling, inequalities, and regression.
outcomes: Identify vertex, axis, intercepts, opening, and extremum.
Interpret standard, factored, and vertex forms.
Convert among forms strategically.
Build and interpret quadratic models.
Solve quadratic inequalities and critique quadratic fits.
units.investigation: Build and optimize an area, revenue, or projectile model and interpret all mathematically valid roots.
units.mastery: Students select and convert forms, graph from structure, solve inequalities, and interpret an optimum with units.

units.title: Rational Expressions, Equations, and Variation
units.act: Act X - Tracking where division is allowed
units.role: Develop algebra with variable denominators, explicit restrictions, and inverse variation.
units.governingQuestion: What changes when a variable expression appears in a denominator?
units.storyArc: A denominator creates excluded inputs. Factoring enables cancellation but cannot restore missing domain points. Common denominators permit addition and equation solving; sign analysis introduces rational inequalities and discontinuities.
outcomes: Identify excluded values and preserve original restrictions.
Simplify and perform arithmetic with rational expressions.
Solve rational equations and check candidate solutions.
Simplify complex rational expressions.
Model variation and interpret holes and asymptotes informally.
units.investigation: Compare equivalent-looking rational formulas and explain how a missing input changes the graph or context.
units.mastery: Every answer must include restrictions and rational-equation candidates must be checked in the original equation.

units.title: Radicals, Rational Exponents, and Complex Numbers
units.shortTitle: Radicals, Rational Exponents, and Complex Numbers
units.act: Act XI - Reversing powers and enlarging the number system
units.role: Develop exact root arithmetic, radical equations, extraneous-solution logic, and basic complex arithmetic.
units.governingQuestion: How do we reverse powers, and what happens when the real numbers are insufficient?
units.storyArc: General roots and rational exponents express inverse powers. Radical arithmetic creates exact forms, conjugates rationalize denominators, and raising powers solves equations but may introduce candidates. Complex numbers complete quadratic solutions.
outcomes: Interpret principal and general roots.
Simplify and combine radical expressions.
Rationalize denominators using factors or conjugates.
Connect radicals and rational exponents.
Solve radical equations and perform basic complex arithmetic.
units.investigation: Compare reversible and nonreversible algebraic steps and explain exactly where extraneous candidates enter.
units.mastery: Students preserve domains, simplify exact forms, check radical candidates, and express nonreal quadratic roots correctly.

units.title: Functions as a Unifying Language
units.act: Act XII - Organizing algebra around input and output
units.role: Consolidate earlier relationships into function language without preempting full Precalculus theory.
units.governingQuestion: How can one input-output framework organize the algebraic families already studied?
units.storyArc: Relations become functions when each input has one output. Function notation separates evaluation from solving; domain and range collect restrictions and outputs; piecewise functions and arithmetic unify earlier examples.
outcomes: Determine whether a relation is a function.
Evaluate functions and solve output equations.
Determine domain and range from formulas, graphs, and contexts.
Interpret graph behavior and piecewise rules.
Combine functions arithmetically while tracking domain.
units.investigation: Choose among linear, quadratic, rational, radical, and exponential models for unlabeled data or graphs.
units.mastery: Students move among table, graph, formula, and context and distinguish evaluation from solving.

units.title: Exponential and Logarithmic Algebra
units.act: Act XIII - Describing multiplicative change and undoing it
units.role: Complete the Algebra course with repeated proportional change, inverse exponentiation, and equation solving.
units.governingQuestion: How do we describe multiplicative change and solve for an unknown exponent?
units.storyArc: Constant differences are contrasted with constant ratios. Repeated percentages produce exponential models, compounding motivates e, and logarithms reverse exponentiation. Log laws follow from exponent laws and solve previously inaccessible equations.
outcomes: Distinguish additive from multiplicative patterns.
Construct and interpret exponential growth and decay models.
Use compound and continuous growth formulas.
Define logarithms as inverse exponentiation and use log laws.
Solve exponential and logarithmic equations with domain checks.
units.investigation: Compare linear, exponential, and logarithmic claims made from the same data and decide which conclusions are justified.
units.mastery: Students construct models, solve exact and approximate equations, and reject logarithmic candidates outside the domain.

units.title: Algebra Synthesis and Precalculus Readiness
units.act: Finale - Choosing structure instead of chapter labels
units.role: Turn accumulated techniques into independent classification, strategy, checking, and modeling.
units.governingQuestion: When the problem is unlabeled, how do we decide what structure it has and what method applies?
units.storyArc: Students classify objects and equation families, choose transformations, track implications and restrictions, use technology responsibly, and complete a sustained model that coordinates words, pictures, graphs, and symbols.
outcomes: Classify mathematical objects and equation families.
Choose productive and legal transformations.
Track restrictions, candidates, and extraneous solutions.
Decide between exact, approximate, algebraic, and graphical answers.
Complete a sustained Precalculus-readiness modeling argument.
units.investigation: A final modeling capstone requiring variable definition, diagram, model selection, solution, restrictions, units, graph, sensitivity, and written conclusion.
units.mastery: Readiness requires success across symbolic fluency, representations, explanation, and modeling; a hidden prerequisite failure routes to targeted review.

exposition: Interpret sign as position, direction, and change; compare signed numbers and rewrite subtraction as addition of an opposite. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In number lines and signed quantities, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Draggable number line with direction arrows and opposite pairs. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Context strip connecting temperature, elevation, and balance to signed values. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unitLessons.title: Fractions as numbers
unitLessons.outcome: Interpret a fraction as a number, quotient, ratio, and operator and locate it on a number line.

opening.prompt: Compare one-half of different-sized objects and locate both on a common scale.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make fractions as numbers necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for fractions as numbers.
exposition: Interpret a fraction as a number, quotient, ratio, and operator and locate it on a number line. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In fractions as numbers, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Fraction strip aligned to a number line. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Area model and quotient model for the same fraction. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

opening.prompt: Represent the same discount as a fraction, decimal, and percent.

exposition: Translate among equivalent representations and choose the form most useful for a question. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In fractions, decimals, and percents, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Hundred grid linked to decimal and percent notation. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Number-line alignment of mixed forms. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unitLessons.title: Units and dimensional reasoning
unitLessons.outcome: Treat units as multiplicative factors that constrain valid operations and conversions.

opening.prompt: Convert a travel speed and test whether a proposed formula has sensible units.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make units and dimensional reasoning necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for units and dimensional reasoning.
exposition: Treat units as multiplicative factors that constrain valid operations and conversions. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In units and dimensional reasoning, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Unit-cancellation chain. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Conversion network. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

examples.prompt: A recipe uses 3 cups of water for 5 cups of flour. Find the water needed for 20 cups of flour.
steps: Write the ordered ratio 3/5 = w/20.
Multiply both sides by 20.
Check that 12/20 reduces to 3/5.
examples.answer: 12 cups of water
examples.interpretation: The scale factor from 5 to 20 is 4, so the water quantity also scales by 4.

unit.title: Arithmetic Readiness and Repair
unit.act: Prologue - Making quantity dependable
unit.role: Adaptive support layer with complete instruction for students who need numerical repair.
unit.governingQuestion: What must be dependable about numbers before symbols can carry meaning?
unit.storyArc: The learner stabilizes numerical meaning: signed quantities, multiplicative structure, fractions, rates, units, powers, and roots. Diagnostic routing allows a student to enter only the pages needed and then return to the main Algebra spine.
outcomes: Interpret signed numbers as position, direction, and change.
Compute with whole numbers, fractions, decimals, and percentages while estimating plausibility.
Use factors, multiples, ratios, rates, and units structurally.
Interpret powers and roots and use scientific notation.
Recognize when arithmetic output is unreasonable or dimensionally impossible.
unit.investigation: Compare several phone, grocery, or subscription plans using estimation, rates, percentages, units, and exact calculations.
unit.mastery: A ten-domain diagnostic routes each missed strand to one repair lesson followed by a short return check.

opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make number lines and signed quantities necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for number lines and signed quantities.
exposition: Interpret sign as position, direction, and change; compare signed numbers and rewrite subtraction as addition of an opposite. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In number lines and signed quantities, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Draggable number line with direction arrows and opposite pairs. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Context strip connecting temperature, elevation, and balance to signed values. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

examples.prompt: Solve and represent −2x + 3 > 7.

lesson.title: Fractions as numbers
lesson.outcome: Interpret a fraction as a number, quotient, ratio, and operator and locate it on a number line.

opening.prompt: Compare one-half of different-sized objects and locate both on a common scale.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make fractions as numbers necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for fractions as numbers.
exposition: Interpret a fraction as a number, quotient, ratio, and operator and locate it on a number line. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In fractions as numbers, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Fraction strip aligned to a number line. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Area model and quotient model for the same fraction. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

examples.prompt: A recipe uses 3 cups of water for 5 cups of flour. Find the water needed for 20 cups of flour.
steps: Write the ordered ratio 3/5 = w/20.
Multiply both sides by 20.
Check that 12/20 reduces to 3/5.
examples.answer: 12 cups of water
examples.interpretation: The scale factor from 5 to 20 is 4, so the water quantity also scales by 4.

examples.interpretation: The second form must communicate the same relationship, not merely repeat the symbols from the first form.

unit.governingQuestion: What must be dependable about numbers before symbols can carry meaning?
unit.storyArc: The learner stabilizes numerical meaning: signed quantities, multiplicative structure, fractions, rates, units, powers, and roots. Diagnostic routing allows a student to enter only the pages needed and then return to the main Algebra spine.
outcomes: Interpret signed numbers as position, direction, and change.

lesson.title: Adding, subtracting, and complex fractions
lesson.outcome: Use common-sized parts to combine fractions and simplify expressions containing fractions within fractions.

opening.prompt: Combine partial quantities measured in different unit fractions.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make adding, subtracting, and complex fractions necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for adding, subtracting, and complex fractions.
exposition: Use common-sized parts to combine fractions and simplify expressions containing fractions within fractions. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In adding, subtracting, and complex fractions, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Unlike fraction strips repartitioned into common units. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

LCM-to-LCD bridge. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

examples.prompt: A recipe uses 3 cups of water for 5 cups of flour. Find the water needed for 20 cups of flour.
steps: Write the ordered ratio 3/5 = w/20.

opening.prompt: Compare prices, speeds, and before-after quantities.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.

exposition: Distinguish ratios from rates, build equivalent comparisons, and interpret percent increase or decrease. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In ratios, rates, proportions, and percent change, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Double number line. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Ratio table with constant multiplier. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Repeated-factor chain. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Square and cube geometry. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unit.title: Arithmetic Readiness and Repair
unit.act: Prologue - Making quantity dependable
unit.role: Adaptive support layer with complete instruction for students who need numerical repair.
unit.governingQuestion: What must be dependable about numbers before symbols can carry meaning?
unit.storyArc: The learner stabilizes numerical meaning: signed quantities, multiplicative structure, fractions, rates, units, powers, and roots. Diagnostic routing allows a student to enter only the pages needed and then return to the main Algebra spine.
outcomes: Interpret signed numbers as position, direction, and change.
Compute with whole numbers, fractions, decimals, and percentages while estimating plausibility.
Use factors, multiples, ratios, rates, and units structurally.
Interpret powers and roots and use scientific notation.
Recognize when arithmetic output is unreasonable or dimensionally impossible.
unit.investigation: Compare several phone, grocery, or subscription plans using estimation, rates, percentages, units, and exact calculations.
unit.mastery: A ten-domain diagnostic routes each missed strand to one repair lesson followed by a short return check.

unit.title: Arithmetic Readiness and Repair
unit.act: Prologue - Making quantity dependable
unit.role: Adaptive support layer with complete instruction for students who need numerical repair.
unit.governingQuestion: What must be dependable about numbers before symbols can carry meaning?
unit.storyArc: The learner stabilizes numerical meaning: signed quantities, multiplicative structure, fractions, rates, units, powers, and roots. Diagnostic routing allows a student to enter only the pages needed and then return to the main Algebra spine.
outcomes: Interpret signed numbers as position, direction, and change.
Compute with whole numbers, fractions, decimals, and percentages while estimating plausibility.
Use factors, multiples, ratios, rates, and units structurally.
Interpret powers and roots and use scientific notation.
Recognize when arithmetic output is unreasonable or dimensionally impossible.
unit.investigation: Compare several phone, grocery, or subscription plans using estimation, rates, percentages, units, and exact calculations.
unit.mastery: A ten-domain diagnostic routes each missed strand to one repair lesson followed by a short return check.

unitLessons.title: Variables and changing quantities
unitLessons.outcome: Distinguish unknowns, changing quantities, parameters, constants, and labels.

opening.prompt: Track altitude over time and decide which quantities vary.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make variables and changing quantities necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for variables and changing quantities.
exposition: Distinguish unknowns, changing quantities, parameters, constants, and labels. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In variables and changing quantities, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Time-altitude table and graph. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Quantity-role map. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unitLessons.title: Substitution and evaluation
unitLessons.outcome: Replace variables or subexpressions with equal-valued expressions while preserving grouping.

opening.prompt: Evaluate a cost formula for several signed and fractional inputs.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make substitution and evaluation necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for substitution and evaluation.
exposition: Replace variables or subexpressions with equal-valued expressions while preserving grouping. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In substitution and evaluation, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Replaceable expression tiles. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Parentheses guard around substituted values. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

lesson.title: Variables and changing quantities
lesson.outcome: Distinguish unknowns, changing quantities, parameters, constants, and labels.

opening.prompt: Track altitude over time and decide which quantities vary.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make variables and changing quantities necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for variables and changing quantities.
exposition: Distinguish unknowns, changing quantities, parameters, constants, and labels. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In variables and changing quantities, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Time-altitude table and graph. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Quantity-role map. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

lesson.title: Properties of real-number operations
lesson.outcome: Use commutative, associative, identity, inverse, and distributive properties to justify rewrites.

opening.prompt: Rearrange a calculation to make it easier without changing its value.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make properties of real-number operations necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for properties of real-number operations.
exposition: Use commutative, associative, identity, inverse, and distributive properties to justify rewrites. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In properties of real-number operations, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Property action cards. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Area model for distribution. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

lesson.title: Formulas, units, and mathematical communication
lesson.outcome: Read formulas as reusable relationships and communicate transformations unambiguously.

opening.prompt: Use an area, distance, or finance formula with units.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make formulas, units, and mathematical communication necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for formulas, units, and mathematical communication.
exposition: Read formulas as reusable relationships and communicate transformations unambiguously. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In formulas, units, and mathematical communication, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Annotated formula with variable meanings and units. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Dimensional-consistency panel. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unit.title: Expressions, Equality, and Linear Equations
unit.act: Act II - Preserving truth while changing form
unit.role: Build the central equivalence engine of elementary algebra.
unit.governingQuestion: How can an equation change form without changing its solutions?
unit.storyArc: Students first test solutions, then use inverse operations and simplification to construct equivalent equations. The unit ends with strategy selection and one-variable modeling.
outcomes: Define a solution and solution set.
Construct equivalent linear equations using legal operations.
Solve equations containing parentheses, fractions, decimals, and variables on both sides.
Recognize identities and contradictions.
Build and check one-variable models.
unit.investigation: Reconstruct an original quantity after a sequence of fees, discounts, or changes.
unit.mastery: Mixed equations without method labels; students must show an equivalence-preserving chain and verify the result.

unitLessons.title: Solutions, solution sets, and checking
unitLessons.outcome: Determine whether candidate values make an equation true and distinguish a proposed answer from a verified solution.

opening.prompt: Test several possible access codes against a condition.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make solutions, solution sets, and checking necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for solutions, solution sets, and checking.
exposition: Determine whether candidate values make an equation true and distinguish a proposed answer from a verified solution. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In solutions, solution sets, and checking, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Left/right value evaluator. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. unitLessons.outcome: Collect variable terms and constants strategically and interpret the resulting coefficient.

opening.prompt: Compare two pricing plans that depend on the same usage variable.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make variables on both sides necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for variables on both sides.
exposition: Collect variable terms and constants strategically and interpret the resulting coefficient. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In variables on both sides, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Variable tiles on both sides. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Choice-of-side comparison. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unitLessons.title: Linear equation strategy studio
unitLessons.outcome: Classify structure, choose a first move, and defend the solution route.

opening.prompt: Sort a mixed set of equations with no chapter labels.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make linear equation strategy studio necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for linear equation strategy studio.
exposition: Classify structure, choose a first move, and defend the solution route. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In linear equation strategy studio, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Equation-family sorter. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Reversible-step map. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unit.title: Expressions, Equality, and Linear Equations
unit.act: Act II - Preserving truth while changing form
unit.role: Build the central equivalence engine of elementary algebra.
unit.governingQuestion: How can an equation change form without changing its solutions?
unit.storyArc: Students first test solutions, then use inverse operations and simplification to construct equivalent equations. The unit ends with strategy selection and one-variable modeling.
outcomes: Define a solution and solution set.
Construct equivalent linear equations using legal operations.
Solve equations containing parentheses, fractions, decimals, and variables on both sides.
Recognize identities and contradictions.
Build and check one-variable models.

unit.mastery: Mixed equations without method labels; students must show an equivalence-preserving chain and verify the result.

opening.prompt: Undo a net change in a balance or temperature.

exposition: Use additive inverses to isolate a variable while preserving equality. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In addition and subtraction equations, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Balance model. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Number-line undoing. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unit.role: Build the central equivalence engine of elementary algebra.
unit.governingQuestion: How can an equation change form without changing its solutions?
unit.storyArc: Students first test solutions, then use inverse operations and simplification to construct equivalent equations. The unit ends with strategy selection and one-variable modeling.

lesson.title: Multistep linear equations
lesson.outcome: Undo layered operations in an order determined by structure.

opening.prompt: Reverse a multi-stage fee or measurement process.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make multistep linear equations necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for multistep linear equations.
exposition: Undo layered operations in an order determined by structure. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In multistep linear equations, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Reverse-operation flowchart. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Equivalent-equation ladder. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

lesson.title: Variables on both sides
lesson.outcome: Collect variable terms and constants strategically and interpret the resulting coefficient.

opening.prompt: Compare two pricing plans that depend on the same usage variable.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make variables on both sides necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for variables on both sides.
exposition: Collect variable terms and constants strategically and interpret the resulting coefficient. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In variables on both sides, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Variable tiles on both sides. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Choice-of-side comparison. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.
